strengths: Addresses an important robotics bottleneck: deriving symbolic planning domains and connecting them to motion planning with limited demonstrations.
The integration of simulation-based predicate discovery, LLM action induction, and constraint grounding is promising and produces interpretable planning representations.

Reports substantial simulation results across nine environments and over 1,200 tasks: 93.3% overall success versus 52.5% for the strongest GPT-4o planning baseline and 95.7% for expert-refined domains.
Evaluates larger object counts, compositional transfer, multiple planning budgets, and prompt variations. Demonstrations on three robot platforms provide additional evidence of practical feasibility.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish the central domain-learning contribution. Most baselines directly generate plans with LLMs; no competing predicate-invention or planning-domain-inference method is evaluated using the same symbolic solver. RuleAsMem primarily demonstrates the benefit of symbolic search. Ablations removing simulation, LLM predicate selection, or domain refinement are missing.

LoCA's claimed semantic guarantee is unsupported. Section 5.2 retrieves constraints only from first-order action effects, without explaining how negative or quantified effects, grasp attachments, contact transitions, and preservation of unaffected predicates are handled. Satisfying endpoint inequalities alone does not establish correct executable manipulation.

Critical implementation details remain unspecified: simulation sampling budgets and feasibility tests, feature bounds and partition widths, bounds on predicate composition, trajectory segmentation, and candidate-domain validation. The manuscript also does not clearly separate refinement problems from held-out evaluation problems.

The single-demonstration and fully automatic claims need qualification. Rearrangement and bridge building combine multiple demonstrations; the system additionally relies on thousands of simulations, supplied object features and CAD models, user-dependent partition sizes, and task descriptions. The VLA deployment uses a policy fine-tuned on 200 trajectories.

Domain-quality evaluation is not independent: expert reference domains are produced by editing PDDLLM outputs, and missing/redundant elements are defined through downstream performance. This does not adequately establish action-model correctness or generalization beyond tested configurations.

Efficiency claims lack complete accounting of offline simulation, domain generation, and candidate selection, together with a clear amortization protocol. Table 2 also shows higher token consumption than both reasoning baselines on Hanoi and bridge building, so the broad token-efficiency claim requires qualification.

Real-robot evaluation is qualitative, without trial counts, success rates, or systematic failure analysis. The suboptimal-demonstration experiment tests missing or additional actions rather than realistic trajectory or perception noise, leaving deployment robustness insufficiently characterized.

strengths: The paper addresses an important robotics bottleneck: constructing symbolic planning domains and connecting them to motion planning. Combining simulation-derived predicate constraints, demonstration-based action induction, and symbolic search is a useful systems direction.

The reported simulation performance is strong: 93.3% overall success across more than 1,200 tasks in nine environments, compared with 52.5% for LLMTAMP-FF and 95.7% for expert-refined domains. Experiments include increasing object counts, alternative planning budgets, and reasoning-model baselines.

The appendix provides prompt templates and additional sensitivity experiments. Demonstrations on three robot platforms and integration with a learned policy provide preliminary evidence of implementation feasibility.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not adequately evaluate the central contribution of domain induction. Most baselines generate action sequences directly, whereas PDDLLM uses a symbolic solver. There are no empirical comparisons with the cited predicate-invention or planning-domain-generation methods under appropriately matched inputs. RuleAsMem mainly establishes the benefit of symbolic search; it does not isolate the benefits of simulation, predicate imagination, action invention, or LoCA.

LoCA's claimed guarantee of semantic alignment is unsupported. Section 5.2 retrieves constraints for first-order action effects, but does not explain sufficiently how negative and quantified effects, grasp/release transitions, preservation of unaffected relations, and trajectory-level requirements are enforced. Satisfying selected endpoint inequalities does not establish execution of the complete symbolic transition. This is a central technical gap, not merely a missing theoretical guarantee.

Predicate construction lacks an adequate account of abstraction validity. A feature subspace is retained when it contains physically feasible samples, but this does not establish that its boundaries define a reliable predicate throughout that subspace. The paper does not quantify classification errors or sensitivity to partition resolution. Appendix A.10's proposed decomposition of higher-dimensional features also does not establish that relevant cross-feature dependencies are preserved.

The automation and single-demonstration claims need qualification. The pipeline assumes structured object states, selected feature spaces and bounds, user-dependent partition sizes, and an available simulator; real-world collection additionally uses CAD models and ArUco markers. Rearrangement and bridge building combine demonstrations from multiple subtasks. The VLA deployment uses a policy fine-tuned on 200 trajectories. These assumptions can be reasonable, but the broad claims of construction without manual predesign or training data obscure the actual scope.

Domain-quality assessment is not independent: the expert reference domains are obtained by refining PDDLLM outputs. Missing/redundant predicate counts against this reference do not establish correctness of learned preconditions and effects on unseen transitions. The candidate-refinement procedure also leaves unclear which problems validate candidates and how those problems are separated from evaluation tasks.

Efficiency claims need clearer accounting. Offline simulation and domain-generation time are not reported alongside online planning time, and token aggregation and amortization are insufficiently explained. Table 2 shows PDDLLM consuming more tokens than both reasoning baselines on Hanoi and bridge building, despite the broad claim of significantly fewer tokens. Exact task counts and aggregation weights are also needed to interpret the overall results.

Real-robot evidence is qualitative: the appendix presents successful sequences without trial counts, success rates, baseline comparisons, or intervention statistics. Reproduction is further limited by missing executable domain examples and insufficient detail on simulation sampling, partition settings, symbolic compilation, and motion-constraint implementation. Consequently, the promising aggregate results do not yet provide sufficient support for the paper's main technical and generality claims at a top-tier venue.

strengths: Addresses an important bottleneck in task and motion planning: constructing symbolic domains and connecting them to execution. Combining simulation-grounded predicate generation with demonstration-based action induction is a promising approach.

The reported simulation results are strong: 93.3% overall success across more than 1,200 tasks in nine environments, compared with 95.7% for expert-refined domains and 52.5% for the strongest GPT-4o planning baseline.

Evaluation includes increasing object counts, compositional transfer, different planning time limits, reasoning-model baselines, and demonstration-coverage experiments. These provide useful evidence beyond a single benchmark setting.
Demonstrations on three robot platforms support practical feasibility. The appendix provides prompt templates and additional experimental results.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish the central domain-induction contribution against closely related methods. Most baselines generate action sequences directly with LLMs; outperforming them primarily demonstrates the benefit of symbolic search. No evaluated baseline learns a domain and uses the same symbolic and motion planners, despite relevant domain-learning approaches being discussed.

LoCA is insufficiently specified to substantiate fully automatic grounding or the claimed semantic guarantee. Retrieving inequalities for first-order action effects does not explain how grasp attachment, release, contact transitions, negative or quantified effects, and preservation of unaffected relations are handled. The manuscript needs a concrete executable mapping and validation of these cases.

Critical domain-generation details remain unclear: simulation sample counts and feasibility criteria, partition settings, bounds on logical-expression enumeration, transition segmentation, and candidate-domain validation. Section 5.1.3 describes replacing domains that fail planning, whereas Appendix A.7 primarily describes voting on predicate names and relevance. The validation tasks and separation from evaluation tasks are not specified.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed innovations. RuleAsMem removes symbolic search, but there are no controlled evaluations removing simulation filtering, replacing LLM predicate naming with fixed interval predicates, or varying partition resolution. Consequently, the necessity and robustness of the predicate-imagination mechanism remain uncertain.

The automation and single-demonstration claims need qualification. The system assumes structured state features, user-selected partition widths, simulator-accessible object models, and accurate state tracking. Rearrangement and bridge building combine demonstrations from multiple subtasks. These are reasonable assumptions, but they narrow the headline claims substantially.

Efficiency claims need clearer accounting. Offline domain derivation uses substantial simulation and LLM computation, but end-to-end costs and amortization assumptions are not adequately reported. Table 2 shows higher PDDLLM token usage than both reasoning baselines for Hanoi and bridge building, so token savings are not consistent across tasks.

Domain-quality and deployment evidence have limitations. Expert reference domains are refinements of the generated domains rather than independent references; missing-predicate rates reach 22.2% in two domains. Real-robot results lack trial counts and success rates, and the VLA demonstration uses a policy fine-tuned on 200 trajectories. These results demonstrate feasibility but do not establish broadly reliable deployment.

strengths: Addresses an important TAMP bottleneck: constructing symbolic domains and connecting learned predicates to motion planning. Combining simulation-grounded predicate generation, demonstration-based action induction, and reusable symbolic planning is a useful system direction.

Reports substantial performance gains across nine task categories: 93.3% overall success versus 52.5% for LLMTAMP-FF, approaching the refined expert baseline’s 95.7%. Experiments include increasing object counts and composition of actions from simpler demonstrations.

Provides physical deployment evidence across three robot platforms, with 7–9 successes out of 10 trials per evaluated task. The appendix also includes useful prompt templates and sensitivity studies covering discretization, parallel prompting, planning budgets, and LLM backbones.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish the central domain-learning contribution against relevant alternatives. Most baselines generate plans directly with an LLM; none evaluates a competing predicate/action induction or LLM domain-generation method using the same symbolic solver and motion planner. RuleAsMem primarily demonstrates the benefit of symbolic search. Ablations removing simulation grounding or replacing the proposed predicate-generation procedure are also missing.

The claimed automatic motion interface and semantic guarantee are insufficiently substantiated. Section 5.2 retrieves constraints for first-order action effects, but does not explain how it handles quantified or negative effects, preserves unaffected predicates, or constructs grasp/release and attachment transitions. Satisfying selected endpoint inequalities does not by itself guarantee correct execution of a symbolic action. A complete executable example and explicit assumptions are needed.

The domain-selection protocol leaves an important evaluation ambiguity. Candidates are discarded for execution failures, including failure to reach goals, but the validation tasks and their separation from test tasks are unspecified. Table 15 reports an 8.3% domain-generation failure rate at the default ten prompts, contradicting the adjacent claim of consistent generation with five or more prompts. It is unclear whether headline success rates include these failures or condition on successful domain generation.

Several essential implementation details remain unspecified despite the extensive appendix: simulation sampling budgets and feasibility criteria, bounds on higher-order predicate enumeration, action-transition segmentation, executable PDDL compilation, and the concrete LoCA-to-planner interface. Illustrative action definitions use informal rather than directly executable PDDL. These gaps make both reproducibility and the extent of manual engineering difficult to assess.

The automation and single-demonstration claims require qualification. The system additionally assumes structured object features, CAD/URDF geometry, a suitable simulator, and substantial simulated experience; rearrangement and bridge building use multiple demonstrations. The VLA experiment additionally uses 200 fine-tuning trajectories. These are reasonable engineering assumptions, but the paper does not quantify the setup effort or sufficiently delimit its claims of construction from scratch.

Efficiency and domain-quality claims are stronger than the evidence. Offline derivation latency and simulation cost are not reported alongside online planning times, and token-cost comparisons lack a clear amortization denominator. Table 2 actually shows higher PDDLLM token costs than both reasoning baselines for Hanoi and bridge building. Furthermore, expert domains are refinements of PDDLLM outputs, making them a useful repair reference but not an independent ground truth for completeness or optimality.

strengths: Addresses an important robotics bottleneck: constructing symbolic planning domains and connecting them to continuous execution. Combining simulation-grounded predicates, demonstration-based action induction, and symbolic search is a useful system direction.

Reports substantial gains across nine task categories: 93.3% overall success versus 52.5% for the strongest GPT-4o planning baseline, with experiments covering increasing object counts and multiple planning budgets.

The appendix provides meaningful additional evidence, including discretization and prompting ablations, smaller-model results, and real-robot evaluations with 7–9 successes in 10 trials across four platform/task settings.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish the central domain-learning contribution. Most baselines generate plans directly with LLMs, whereas PDDLLM uses a symbolic solver. There are no experimental comparisons with the closely related domain-inference and predicate-learning methods discussed in Section 2. RuleAsMem mainly demonstrates the benefit of symbolic search; it does not isolate the benefits of simulation-grounded predicate generation or LoCA.

The claimed automatic motion-grounding guarantee is insufficiently justified. Section 5.2 retrieves constraints from first-order action effects, but does not adequately explain handling of negative or quantified effects, grasp/contact transitions, or preservation of unaffected relations. Satisfying selected endpoint inequalities does not establish executable action semantics. Likewise, finding feasible samples within a discretized region does not establish feasibility throughout that region.

Important implementation details remain unspecified despite the extensive appendix: simulation sample counts and feasibility criteria, finite bounds on higher-order predicate enumeration, transition segmentation, and the actual PDDL/PDDLStream compilation and constraint interface. The displayed action examples contain nonstandard PDDL notation, without complete executable domains demonstrating how it is resolved.

Domain validation and quality assessment need stronger independence. Candidate domains are filtered using execution and goal-reaching feedback, but the validation tasks and their separation from evaluation tasks are unclear. Expert reference domains are edits of PDDLLM outputs, limiting their independence as a quality benchmark. Missing/redundant predicate counts also do not directly assess action-model soundness on unseen transitions.

The efficiency claims need qualification and complete accounting. Online planning excludes offline domain construction, while simulation and derivation wall-clock costs are not reported. Table 2 shows PDDLLM consuming more tokens than both reasoning baselines for Hanoi and bridge building, contrary to the broad claim of consistently lower consumption. The evaluation should specify the amortization workload and report end-to-end costs.

The single-demonstration and full-automation framing overstates the demonstrated scope. Rearrangement and bridge building use multiple demonstrations; the system additionally assumes structured features, CAD/URDF models, simulation, and tracked object states. The VLA experiment uses 200 fine-tuning trajectories and bypasses LoCA, so it supports modular compatibility rather than automatic constraint grounding.

Some reliability claims conflict with the reported evidence. Appendix B.16 states that five or more prompts consistently produce executable domains, but Table 15 reports an 8.3% failure rate at both five and ten prompts. It is unclear how these domain-generation failures enter the headline planning success rates. This uncertainty, together with the missing comparisons and grounding details, prevents the reported gains from establishing a sufficiently convincing top-tier contribution.

strengths: Addresses an important TAMP bottleneck: constructing symbolic domains and connecting them to motion planning. Combining simulation-grounded predicate generation, demonstration-based action induction, and reusable symbolic planning is practically appealing.

Reports substantial improvements across more than 1,200 problems in nine environments: 93.3% overall success versus 52.5% for the strongest GPT-4o planning baseline and 95.7% for expert-refined domains.

Provides useful evidence of generalization to larger object counts and composition of demonstrated skills. Real-robot evaluations span three platforms, with 7–9 successes out of 10 trials across four settings.

The appendix contains substantial supporting material, including prompts, time-budget comparisons, alternative LLM backbones, discretization and parallel-prompt ablations, and perception-noise experiments.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish the central domain-learning contribution against relevant alternatives. There are no empirical comparisons with cited predicate-invention or LLM-based domain-generation methods. Most baselines generate action sequences directly, so the large gains may primarily reflect the advantage of symbolic search. RuleAsMem tests the solver contribution, but ablations removing simulation grounding or replacing the proposed domain-generation procedure are missing.

LoCA's claimed automatic grounding and semantic guarantee are insufficiently established. Section 5.2 describes retrieving inequalities from first-order effects, but does not specify how negative and quantified effects, grasp attachments, contact transitions, or preservation of unaffected relations are handled. Satisfying selected endpoint inequalities alone does not guarantee executable actions with the intended semantics. These details are central to the claimed removal of manually engineered skills.

Several essential domain-construction steps remain underspecified despite the extensive appendix: simulation sampling budgets and feasibility criteria, the finite grammar and depth of higher-order predicate enumeration, action-transition segmentation, and compilation into valid executable PDDL. Retaining a subspace because it contains some feasible samples also does not establish feasibility throughout that subspace.

The evaluation protocol leaves consequential uncertainties. Candidate domains are filtered using execution feedback, but the validation problems and their separation from final evaluation are not clearly specified. Table 15 reports an 8.3% domain-generation failure rate at the default ten prompts; it is unclear whether these failures count toward the headline success rates. Furthermore, the expert reference is obtained by editing the proposed method's outputs, limiting its independence as a domain-quality benchmark.

Efficiency claims need clearer accounting. Online planning times exclude domain construction, while simulation and domain-generation wall-clock costs are unreported. Table 2 shows higher token consumption than both reasoning baselines for Hanoi and bridge building, despite the broad claim of significantly fewer tokens. Reusable domains plausibly offer amortized savings, but the comparison needs a defined deployment workload and break-even analysis.

The single-demonstration and full-automation framing exceeds the demonstrated scope. Rearrangement and bridge building use multiple demonstrations; the system additionally assumes structured object features, CAD models, simulation access, and marker-based state estimates. The VLA deployment uses 200 fine-tuning trajectories and bypasses LoCA, supporting modular compatibility rather than validating automatic constraint grounding. These qualifications, together with the missing comparisons and implementation details, prevent the otherwise promising results from meeting the acceptance threshold.
